THE HUMAN ATLASES · DEEP DIVE

Europe: departures, returns and American connections

Follow the voyages beyond the edge of one regional map. A departure port, an island stop and a return anchorage are parts of the same journey, with the same evidence and the same limits on what can be reconstructed.

This directory connects the existing voyage catalogue across regional guides. It does not add speculative stages or change the shared movie. Representative mapped anchors introduce the area; the complete dated regional list follows below.

One journey across several regions

The dated lists retain each itinerary’s original descriptions. A documented landfall, a roadstead stay and a passage offshore are different kinds of evidence. Where the source leaves a gap, a linking animation is an illustration rather than a recovered daily ship track. [1] [2] [3]

Read departures and returns together

The same port can occur more than once in a journey, and several expeditions can share a harbor. Keeping those visits separate makes it possible to follow preparation, outbound movement and return without turning a port into one timeless event. [1] [2] [3]

Journeys and their documented stops

58 itineraries in the shared catalogue include anchors in this regional collection. Open a journey to follow its existing timeline. Dates and notes below come directly from the same canonical itinerary; a passage or sighting is not automatically a landing.

Columbus: selected first-voyage anchors, 1492–1493

Selected anchors from the surviving Las Casas abstract. The Bahamas landfall and some Caribbean locations remain debated; broad regional anchors are used. Indigenous peoples already inhabited these places. The expedition involved coercion and captivity, and later return legs do not represent Santa María, which was wrecked.

Vicente Yáñez Pinzón’s return voyage

Gaspar Corte-Real’s second fleet · Lisbon evidence

A Portuguese chronicle gives the fleet’s May departure. One of the surviving caravels returned with kidnapped Indigenous people in October, according to a contemporary Lisbon letter. The fleet’s American landfall and the fate of Gaspar’s vessel remain unresolved.

    Pasqualigo’s October letter dates one caravel’s return to the eighth and describes Indigenous captives taken from North America. Gaspar did not return with this ship. The following movement is not reconstructed.

Narváez’s fleet and Florida expedition

Narváez left Spain with a colonizing fleet and wintered in Cuba after a storm damaged the expedition. The land force traveled from the Tampa Bay region into Apalachee and left the Gulf coast in improvised boats. Several sites and sections of the route remain uncertain.

Schouten and Le Maire · Eendracht around Cape Horn to Jacatra

Eendracht (called Unitie in the English account) sailed with Hoorn from the Netherlands to Patagonia. After Hoorn burned at Puerto Deseado, Eendracht passed the strait between Tierra del Fuego and Isla de los Estados and rounded Cape Horn. The Pacific and East Indies stages end at Jacatra, where the VOC seized the ship. The return aboard Amsterdam is a separate itinerary.

Champlain and Indigenous guides · Great Lakes journey and return

Champlain’s own party traveled through the Ottawa–Nipissing–French River corridor to Wendat country, joined an unsuccessful allied campaign, wintered with his hosts and returned via Québec to France.
